segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I was putting, the line in the past?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now if you want to say I put, the point in the past, I put, in the past of course in English it's doesn't change, I put present, I put past. I put for the past, our base is pus-, pus-, P-U-S. So how would you say I put?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The endings don't take the accent here for these irregular verbs. Puse. You put, informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And now we can see where that poner pose was coming from. We said that when we have poner as part of a verb in Spanish it's -pose in English, componer - compose, exponer - expose, oponer - oppose. And now we hear this pos- sound coming out in the dot in the past. Puse, pusiste. What was to to do or to make?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The base here in this point in the past is hic- H-I-C. So if you want to say I made or I did?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And he made or he did?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hizo. Here it would be H-I-Z-O, we can't keep the C because it would spell hico. Hizo. They made or you guys made?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Whenever you identify one of these irregular verbs in the point in the past where the base of the verb has changed, then you know what to do with it. That -e and -o is coming from -ar, and then you have -imos, -iste, -ieron from -er, -ir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Sometimes the change is subtle. We saw that pod- of poder became pud-. We saw in another lesson that hab- of haber became hub-. Ven- of venir becomes vin-. So how would you say I came?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You know how to say wine in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Traer, to bring, has traje, I brought, in the past. So how would you say he brought?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And traje also means suit, like the kind you wear, and it's masculine. So I brought a suit would be?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Traje un traje. Vino con vino, traje un traje.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: There's one extra irregular past point to look at. It's extra irregular because it doesn't really follow these rules about what groups it's taking the sounds from, and it's also extra irregular because it is the past for both ser and ir. It is the past for both I was and I went, and this is fui. F-U-I, fui.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Fui. So fui means I was, from ser, point in the past, and it also means I went. Huh? So ser and ir in the point in the past, they share a past. Fui means I was or I went, and fue means he was, she was, it was, you were, or went. So we see that it's extremely irregular.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Fui, I was or I went, how would you say I didn't go?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No fui. Fue, he was or he went, how would you say he didn't go?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No fue. How would you say we went?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Fuiste. Now to make they or you plural was or went, we would add on -ieron, but we will find it very difficult to pronounce fuieron, fuieron, so the "i" sound, the I, fell away. So how would that sound?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Fueron. So the I, the "i" sound, falls away. Fueron.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The same thing happens in a couple of other cases too. We have trajeron from traer, to bring, they brought, you guys brought, trajeron; dijeron, they or you guys said. So a couple of other examples there of that I falling away just for sound reasons. Trajieron, dijieron is kind of difficult to say, so it fell away for efficiency. Dijeron, trajeron, fueron.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So now that we have fueron, we can make the past mood tense. We can say something like if I were you, because we always go from the they form of the point in the past. So if they went or they were is fueron, we can say if I were you.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And of course we're using the mood tense here because we have if going into the past hypothetically. So this is a mood tense that's quite specific for the past. We're not putting the mood tense after si, after if, in the present, but for this hypothetical past, if I were you, there we have it, in English as well as in Spanish. We said that if I were you instead of if I was you is mood tense in English. So how would that be, if I were you?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: And the I version is fuera.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now it's just the word for you.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tú or usted, depending on who we're talking to. So si yo fuera tú, huh? Si fuera tú, or si yo fuera tú, si yo fuera usted, if I were you.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now we're understanding why we went from the they version to find the mood tense in the past. Because going from the they version instead of the tú form means that if there is some irregularity, we will transfer that irregularity over into the mood tense. So we went from fueron to fuera, and we would go from, for example, dijeron, they spoke, to dijera, so we carry over that irregularity of having lost that I. Trajeron, they brought, and then trajera for the mood tense.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I had was tuve. What was they had or you guys had?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tuvieron. So now we can say if I had it, I would tell you. If I had it, I would tell you.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I would tell you. You can use contar. Decir is very irregular for for would, so if you don't want to deal with that now, imagine you're in a real life context, you can just go to the more regular verb which is contar. I would tell you, informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Si lo tuviera, te contaría. Or te lo contaría, I would tell you it. We like to close with this it in Spanish a lot. Si lo tuviera, te lo contaría, I would tell you it. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So going from this they form of the point in the past, we can easily find the mood tense in the past even if the verb is irregular. So we have to do or to make which is hacer, and we said that the root for the point in the past is hic- H-I-C for the I version. So how would you say I made or I did?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hice. And they did or they made?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you could say I wanted for them to do it. I wanted that they did it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. I wanted them to do it. I wanted that they do it. Quería que lo hicieran. How would you say I wanted for us to do it? I wanted that we do it, that we did it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Well done. Quería que lo hiciéramos. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I'm not as interested here in installing let's say all of this content, all of these irregular verbs. What I want to give you is an exposure to how they might work, the irregular verbs that you can come across, so that practicing you can manage them. So you should not be afraid of making mistakes, you should build the verbs how you're used to, and if you suspect that this one might be irregular, check. Check with the person that you're speaking to.
